data.problem: India's standard meridian is 82.5 degrees East and the Prime Meridian is 0 degrees. When it is 12 noon in Greenwich, what is the Indian Standard Time?

steps.why: Simply the difference between 82.5 East and 0, since they are on the same side of the grid.

steps.ask: How much time does one degree of longitude represent?
steps.why: The Earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours, that is 1440 minutes, and 1440 divided by 360 is 4 minutes per degree.

steps.ask: So what is the total time difference?
steps.why: 82.5 multiplied by 4 is 330 minutes, and 330 minutes is 5 hours 30 minutes.

steps.ask: Is India ahead of Greenwich or behind it?
steps.why: The Sun rises in the east, so places east of the Prime Meridian are ahead in time. East means add, west means subtract.

data.answer: 5.30 pm. India is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich.

steps.why: Carbon 12 plus two oxygens at 16 each, that is 12 + 32 = 44.

steps.ask: What volume would this occupy at STP?
steps.why: One mole of any gas occupies 22.4 litres at STP, so two moles occupy 44.8 litres. Note this holds for any gas, whatever its molecular mass.

steps.ask: Divide 867 by 255. What is the remainder?
Now repeat with 255 and 102. What is the remainder?
steps.why: 102 × 2 = 204, and 255 − 204 = 51. So 255 = 102 × 2 + 51. The rule is always: the old divisor becomes the new dividend.

steps.ask: Repeat once more with 102 and 51.
steps.why: 51 divides 102 exactly twice, so 102 = 51 × 2 + 0. A remainder of zero means we stop.

steps.ask: So what is the HCF?
steps.why: The HCF is the last divisor used before the remainder became zero, which is 51. Check: 867 = 51 × 17 and 255 = 51 × 5.

trick: The midpoint formula is just the section formula with the ratio 1:1, so there is really only one formula to know. And the distance formula is Pythagoras in disguise: the difference in x and the difference in y are the two legs of a right triangle.

data.prompt: Choose the right formula for each task.

items.ask: The distance between (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂)
items.why: Take the differences, square them, add and take the square root. Forgetting the root leaves you with the square of the distance, which is a common slip when the numbers come out neatly.

items.ask: The midpoint of the segment joining (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂)
items.why: The midpoint is the average of the coordinates, so you add and halve. Subtracting gives you half the displacement, not the point.

items.ask: The point dividing the join of (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) in the ratio m:n internally
items.why: The m goes with the second point and the n with the first — cross over, not straight across. Check it by putting m = n = 1: you should get the midpoint back.

items.ask: The area of a triangle with vertices (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂), (x₃, y₃)
items.correct: ½ |x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|
wrong: x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)
items.why: The half and the modulus both matter: area is never negative, so if your value comes out negative, take its size. An area of zero means the three points are collinear, which is how this formula is often used.

We know the hypotenuse and want the opposite

data.prompt: Pick the right formula, and see what rules the others out.

items.ask: Curved surface area of a cylinder of radius r and height h
items.why: Unroll the curved surface and you get a rectangle of width 2πr and height h. πr²h is the volume, and 2πr(r + h) is the total surface area including both circular ends.

items.ask: Curved surface area of a cone of radius r, height h and slant height l
items.why: The curved surface uses the slant height l, not the vertical height h, where l² = r² + h². The third option is the volume.

items.ask: Volume of a sphere of radius r
items.why: The one with r³ must be the volume; 4πr² is its surface area. (2/3)πr³ is the volume of a hemisphere, which is half of it.

items.ask: Total surface area of a hemisphere of radius r
items.why: Half the sphere's curved surface is 2πr², and the flat circular face adds another πr², making 3πr². If a question asks only for the curved surface, the answer is 2πr² — read which one is wanted.

trick: Errors add in a fixed way: for a sum or difference you add the absolute errors, for a product or quotient you add the relative errors, and a power multiplies the relative error by that power. So a quantity that is squared contributes twice as much error as one that is not.

data.prompt: True or false? Mark each statement about errors and significant figures.

items.statement: When quantities are added, their absolute errors add.
items.why: Errors never cancel in your favour, so even in a subtraction the absolute errors are added.

items.statement: When quantities are multiplied, their absolute errors add.
items.why: For products and quotients it is the relative or percentage errors that add, not the absolute ones.

items.statement: The number 0.00340 has three significant figures.

items.statement: A systematic error can be reduced by taking many readings.
items.why: Repeating readings averages out random error only. A systematic error, like a zero error in the instrument, shifts every reading the same way.

items.statement: If a quantity is squared in a formula, its relative error is doubled.
items.why: A power n multiplies the relative error by n, which is why the most-powered quantity deserves the most careful measurement.

data.prompt: Choose the right relation for each case.

items.ask: Velocity after time t under constant acceleration
items.why: The first equation of motion. Check it dimensionally: at is acceleration times time, which is a velocity.

items.ask: Displacement after time t under constant acceleration
items.why: The half belongs to the acceleration term because the extra velocity builds up gradually, so its average contribution is half the final one.

items.ask: Maximum height of a projectile launched at angle θ with speed u
items.why: Height depends only on the vertical component u sinθ. The second option is the range, which uses sin 2θ — the single most confused pair in this chapter.

items.ask: Range of a projectile on level ground
items.why: Range uses sin 2θ, which is why 45° gives the maximum range and why 30° and 60° give the same one. The third option is the time of flight.

trick: Draw the free-body diagram before writing a single equation. Most errors in this chapter are not algebra but a force left off the picture, and the commonest one left off is friction acting against the motion, not along it.

data.prompt: True or false? Mark each statement about motion and friction.

items.statement: Newton's third law pair of forces act on two different bodies.
items.why: That is why they never cancel each other. Action and reaction on the same body would leave nothing ever able to accelerate.

items.statement: Limiting friction is greater than kinetic friction.
items.why: It takes more force to start something sliding than to keep it sliding, which is why an object jerks into motion.

items.statement: Friction depends on the area of contact.
items.why: To a good approximation it depends only on the normal reaction and the nature of the surfaces, not on how much area is touching.

items.statement: A body in uniform circular motion has no acceleration.
items.why: Its speed is constant but its direction changes constantly, so there is a centripetal acceleration directed at the centre.

items.statement: Momentum is conserved in every collision, elastic or not.
items.why: Momentum is always conserved when no external force acts. It is kinetic energy that is conserved only in an elastic collision.
